name: QC vs Classical Computing
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Two Machines, Two Jobs: Quantum and Classical Compared
lesson.summary: Directly compares the quantum and classical computing paradigms across their underlying mechanics, complexity classes, and practical architecture, framing quantum processors as specialized coprocessors rather than replacements.
lesson.body:
With the promises and the limits of quantum computing both laid out in the previous two sections, it is worth stepping back and comparing the two paradigms directly. Classical computing, built from bits that are always definitely 0 or 1, executes deterministic sequences of Boolean logic operations, AND, OR, NOT, and their combinations, on transistors that have been engineered and re-engineered for decades to be fast, cheap, and staggeringly reliable. Quantum computing, built from qubits that can be placed in superposition and entangled with one another, executes sequences of reversible unitary operations whose outcomes, upon measurement, are fundamentally probabilistic rather than deterministic. These are not just two different technologies for doing the same thing, they are two different computational models.

Theoretical computer science gives this comparison a formal shape. The class of problems a classical computer can solve efficiently, roughly meaning in time that grows polynomially with input size, is called P. The corresponding class for quantum computers is called BQP, for bounded error quantum polynomial time. Every problem in P is believed to also be in BQP, since a quantum computer can always simulate a classical one. Factoring, thanks to Shor's algorithm, is known to be in BQP and is believed, though not proven, to sit outside P, which is exactly the kind of separation that gives quantum computing its edge on that specific problem. But as the previous section stressed, BQP is believed not to contain NP-complete problems, so this edge does not extend to hard problems generally.

In practical terms, the comparison plays out unevenly depending on the task. For everyday arithmetic, logic, data storage, and general purpose software, classical computing wins decisively: it is faster in absolute terms for these tasks, vastly cheaper, and does not require the extreme physical isolation that qubits do. For a narrow set of mathematically structured problems, factoring large integers, simulating certain quantum mechanical systems, and possibly some optimization and sampling tasks, quantum computing offers a proven or plausible advantage, provided the hardware exists to realize it at sufficient scale and low enough error.

This uneven comparison points toward the architecture that most researchers actually expect: not quantum computers replacing classical ones, but quantum processors acting as specialized coprocessors that a classical system calls on for specific subroutines, similar in spirit, as a loose analogy, to how a graphics processing unit, or GPU, accelerates certain parallel numerical workloads inside an otherwise classical computer without replacing its central processor. Many current quantum algorithms, including the optimization heuristics mentioned earlier, are explicitly hybrid: a classical computer manages the overall problem and repeatedly calls a quantum processor to evaluate a piece that benefits from superposition and entanglement.

None of this changes the fact that, for the moment, classical computing remains overwhelmingly more capable across nearly every practical task, including many of the specific applications claimed for quantum computers. The reason has less to do with algorithms and more to do with physics: qubits are extraordinarily difficult to build, control, and keep coherent, and the remaining sections of this chapter turn to exactly why that is, starting with the decoherence problem that grows directly out of the measurement problem covered earlier.
